findings:
  - { id: judged-forge-429-errunavailable, kind: judged, text: "ac-2 declares 'HTTP 429 classifies as ErrUnavailable so rate limits route to the degrade/retry path', but only the Jira adapter delivers it: internal/provider/jira/jira.go's classify wraps 429 (and 5xx, and transport errors) in provider.ErrUnavailable, while the GitHub and GitLab forge classifiers (internal/forge/github/github.go classify/classifyPost ~lines 220-250, internal/forge/gitlab/gitlab.go ~lines 200-230) return plain fmt.Errorf 'rate limited: status ...' errors with no sentinel, and internal/forge defines no unavailable-style sentinel to wrap. Callers cannot errors.Is a forge rate limit, so forge-side 429s remain string-distinguishable generic failures that never reach a degrade/retry path. Both forge adapters' comments openly state the deviation ('429 named as rate-limited, since forge carries no unavailable-style sentinel today — spec/forge-transport ac-3') — and cite the same forge-transport clause the Jira adapter cites to justify the OPPOSITE behavior (routing 429 to ErrUnavailable), so the two readings of that clause are mutually inconsistent. Every mechanical check (429 specially recognized, shared httpjson seam, deadlines, pagination drained to exhaustion including GitHub's nested thread-comments cursor) holds; the routing semantic is what's missing on two of the three adapters. (confidence 0.65)", disposition: accepted-deviation, note: "Accepted: the archived, closed spec/forge-transport's frozen ac-3 is the story-level refinement of this feature AC's shorthand, and its text IS the split the finding reads as inconsistency — 'HTTP 429 classifies to the unavailable sentinel in the shared classifier (provider.ErrUnavailable on the tracker side, the forge side's transient refusal naming the status)'. The Jira adapter implements the first half; the github/gitlab classifiers implement the second, and their comments cite the clause correctly — two halves of one ratified sentence, not two readings of it. The forge side's degrade path is the consumer-level one the closure gate already exercises (buildForgeBestEffort → disclosed-unproven, never a hard failure). A forge-side sentinel remains a reasonable future widening; it would be a new mechanism beyond both frozen contracts, not a missing piece of either." }

These fall outside the audit's witnessed ten (they hash raw bytes, not canonical JSON), so the letter of ac-3 holds, but 'one home per shared behavior' is undercut for the digest-string format itself: a future change to the prefix or encoding must now be found in five places (canonjson plus these four). Also witness-scoped on the merits, as the finding itself concedes: dc-2/co-3 bound ac-3's extractions to the audit's witnessed list — the ten canonjson→sha256 copies — and these four are raw-bytes digests outside that list, which canonjson.Digest's canonical-JSON signature genuinely cannot serve. The residual is real: the 'sha256:'+hex format now lives in five places. Named follow-up: a raw-bytes sibling (e.g. canonjson.DigestBytes) sweeping the four copies, ordinary hygiene work for a future pass, with the parity guarded by a test per the one-source-of-truth rule." }

## Judged

- **judged-forge-429-errunavailable** [accepted-deviation]: ac-2 declares 'HTTP 429 classifies as ErrUnavailable so rate limits route to the degrade/retry path', but only the Jira adapter delivers it: internal/provider/jira/jira.go's classify wraps 429 (and 5xx, and transport errors) in provider.ErrUnavailable, while the GitHub and GitLab forge classifiers (internal/forge/github/github.go classify/classifyPost ~lines 220-250, internal/forge/gitlab/gitlab.go ~lines 200-230) return plain fmt.Errorf 'rate limited: status ...' errors with no sentinel, and internal/forge defines no unavailable-style sentinel to wrap. Callers cannot errors.Is a forge rate limit, so forge-side 429s remain string-distinguishable generic failures that never reach a degrade/retry path. Both forge adapters' comments openly state the deviation ('429 named as rate-limited, since forge carries no unavailable-style sentinel today — spec/forge-transport ac-3') — and cite the same forge-transport clause the Jira adapter cites to justify the OPPOSITE behavior (routing 429 to ErrUnavailable), so the two readings of that clause are mutually inconsistent. Every mechanical check (429 specially recognized, shared httpjson seam, deadlines, pagination drained to exhaustion including GitHub's nested thread-comments cursor) holds; the routing semantic is what's missing on two of the three adapters. (confidence 0.65) — Accepted: the archived, closed spec/forge-transport's frozen ac-3 is the story-level refinement of this feature AC's shorthand, and its text IS the split the finding reads as inconsistency — 'HTTP 429 classifies to the unavailable sentinel in the shared classifier (provider.ErrUnavailable on the tracker side, the forge side's transient refusal naming the status)'. The Jira adapter implements the first half; the github/gitlab classifiers implement the second, and their comments cite the clause correctly — two halves of one ratified sentence, not two readings of it. The forge side's degrade path is the consumer-level one the closure gate already exercises (buildForgeBestEffort → disclosed-unproven, never a hard failure). A forge-side sentinel remains a reasonable future widening; it would be a new mechanism beyond both frozen contracts, not a missing piece of either.
- **judged-digest-single-home** [accepted-deviation]: ac-3's 'single digest helper' (canonjson.Digest) collapsed the canonjson→sha256→prefixed-hex copies, but the sibling raw-bytes variant of the same behavior still has four homes producing the identical 'sha256:'+hex.EncodeToString(sum[:]) digest string: internal/workbench/badges.go:179-182 contentDigest and internal/wallbadge/judgedsweep.go:241-244 judgedContentDigest are byte-identical three-line helpers (both documenting the same dc-5 content-revision role), and internal/evidence/records.go:267-268 and internal/evidence/pendingsupersession.go:83-84 inline the same idiom. These fall outside the audit's witnessed ten (they hash raw bytes, not canonical JSON), so the letter of ac-3 holds, but 'one home per shared behavior' is undercut for the digest-string format itself: a future change to the prefix or encoding must now be found in five places (canonjson plus these four). Low confidence because dc-2/co-3 scope fixes to the audit's witness list and a raw-bytes helper genuinely cannot reuse canonjson.Digest's signature — this may be deliberate non-inclusion rather than drift. (confidence 0.35) — Accepted-and-recorded under the R4-I-84 circuit-breaker (this ritual's two fix loops are spent: the comment sweep, then the three-residue pass; a further non-critical finding is adjudicate-and-record). Also witness-scoped on the merits, as the finding itself concedes: dc-2/co-3 bound ac-3's extractions to the audit's witnessed list — the ten canonjson→sha256 copies — and these four are raw-bytes digests outside that list, which canonjson.Digest's canonical-JSON signature genuinely cannot serve. The residual is real: the 'sha256:'+hex format now lives in five places. Named follow-up: a raw-bytes sibling (e.g. canonjson.DigestBytes) sweeping the four copies, ordinary hygiene work for a future pass, with the parity guarded by a test per the one-source-of-truth rule.
